---
title: "Why analytical quality matters at NHSBSA"
description: "The principles this playbook rests on, and what goes wrong when quality is assumed rather than assured."
---

NHSBSA analysis informs how public money is spent, how services are run, and what the public is told.
When it is right, nobody notices. When it is wrong, the cost lands somewhere else and usually later.

## The principles

Six of them. Five are GovS 010's own, which means following them is how NHSBSA meets the standard
rather than something extra on top.[^src-govs-010-section-2] The clause each one answers to is named
beneath it, so you can see which are the standard's and which are NHSBSA's.

::: {.callout-note title="The principles are the mandatory part of GovS 010" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
GovS 010 distinguishes **shall**, a requirement, from **should**, a recommendation. The word *shall*
appears eleven times in the whole document. One of the eleven is the conventions table defining it,
and seven of the remaining ten say that a different functional standard is to be followed: GovS 005
Digital, GovS 008 Commercial or GovS 011 Communication.

**That leaves three substantive requirements.** The six principles below, which the standard puts as
"those engaged in analysis shall ensure"[^src-govs-010-section-2]; NHSBSA having a senior officer
accountable for its analysis activities[^src-govs-010-section-4-1-3]; and analytical roles and
accountabilities being defined in the governance framework and assigned to people with appropriate
seniority, skills and experience[^src-govs-010-section-4-4-1]. The first falls on you. The other two
fall on the organisation, and [section 3](../03-roles-and-responsibilities/index.qmd) is where they
are met.

Everything else the standard asks for is a *should*. That is not permission to skip it. A *should*
you depart from is a decision you have to be able to explain, which is why this playbook asks you
to record the ones you depart from rather than to treat them as optional.
:::

{{< include /guidance/_partials/diagram-govs010.qmd >}}

### 1. Analysis answers the right questions

There should be a clear, shared understanding of the questions to be answered, how they meet user
needs, and **how certain the answer needs to be**. Analysis should be for the public good and aligned
to government policy and organisational objectives.

*GovS 010 principle 1 and section 5.2. See [section 4](../04-analytical-lifecycle/index.qmd),
phase 1.*

### 2. Using the right methods

Analysis uses appropriate inputs and methods to produce high quality results. It should be
repeatable, independent, grounded in reality, objective, with
[uncertainty](../07-uncertainty/index.qmd) understood and managed, and it should answer the original
question robustly. That is **RIGOUR**, set out in full in
[section 2](../02-standards-landscape/index.qmd).

*GovS 010 principle 2, and the AQuA Book. See [section 6](../06-doing-the-work/index.qmd).*

### 3. At the right time

Analysis is provided in time to be useful. **That is never at the expense of quality assurance.**
Where time is genuinely short, the proportionate answer is a narrower question answered properly.

*GovS 010 section 5.5. See [section 5](../05-deciding-your-assurance-level/index.qmd).*

### 4. With the right level of quality assurance

Quality assurance **and continuous improvement** are built into the way analysis is carried out.
Assurance is proportionate to the impact of the results on the decision and to the risks of how they
will be used, and what a review finds goes into the next piece of work.

*GovS 010 principle 4. See [section 5](../05-deciding-your-assurance-level/index.qmd) for the level
and [section 11](../11-review-and-continuous-improvement/index.qmd) for the improvement.*

### 5. Following the right standards

Analysis is undertaken in line with legal and ethical obligations, with public service codes of
conduct, and with those of your own profession.

*GovS 010 principle 5. See [section 2](../02-standards-landscape/index.qmd) for the standards and
[section 10](../10-ethics-and-transparency/index.qmd) for the ethics.*

### 6. Presented in the right way

Analysis supports effective decision-making and meets user needs through clearly presented,
impartial, timely and accessible outputs. That includes being clear about context, strengths,
limitations, and **what remains uncertain, stated plainly enough to act on**.

*GovS 010 principle 3. See [section 9](../09-communicating-analysis/index.qmd) and
[section 7](../07-uncertainty/index.qmd).*

**So the right decisions are made.** Good quality analysis can be trusted to support effective
decision-making and meet user needs. That is the whole of it, and everything else in this playbook
is how.

::: {.callout-important title="Uncertainty is agreed, not just reported" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
**An analysis with no agreed margin of error has no threshold to be tested against**, and a
commissioner who has not been asked how certain the answer needs to be has no grounds for saying an
answer is not good enough.

Agree it at scoping, record it in the analytical plan, design against it, and say at the end what is
still uncertain. [Section 7](../07-uncertainty/index.qmd) is how you measure it.
[Section 4](../04-analytical-lifecycle/index.qmd) is where you agree it.

Three sources ask for the agreement rather than the measurement. GovS 010 asks for the levels of
quality and certainty required to be agreed and recorded at scoping.[^src-govs-010-section-5-2] The AQuA
Book asks analysts at design stage to mine the planned analysis systematically for sources of
uncertainty large enough to breach "the acceptable margin of error", which only means something if
somebody has said what that margin is.[^src-aqua-book-section-7-4] And the
[Uncertainty Toolkit for Analysts](https://analystsuncertaintytoolkit.github.io/UncertaintyWeb/)
gives its whole second chapter to jointly agreeing how uncertainty should be used, before the
analysis is designed. **None of the three is about measuring uncertainty.** They are about agreeing
how much of it the decision can carry, while there is still time to design for it.

Techniques for quantifying uncertainty will keep changing. The agreement will not, which is why it
sits in the principles rather than in a method.
:::

## What goes wrong when quality is assumed

Poor analytical quality rarely announces itself. It shows up in recognisable ways:

**The number outlives its caveat.** A figure is quoted in a paper. The caveat that qualified it sat
in an annex and did not travel. A decision is taken on a number that meant something narrower than
the reader thought.

**The one-off becomes production.** Work built quickly for a single question turns out to be useful
and is rerun for months. Nobody re-assesses anything, because no single moment felt like a decision.

**Assurance is done but not recorded.** Somebody checked. Nobody can now say what they checked, when,
or what they found. The work cannot be defended, and a practice area cannot be evidenced as
compliant.

**Effort goes to the wrong place.** Low-risk work is over-engineered because that is the only
standard anyone has articulated, while high-risk work is thin because it arrived with a deadline.

Each of these is a process failure rather than a competence failure, and each is what this playbook
exists to prevent.

## What NHSBSA has committed to

NHSBSA has committed to being a data-driven organisation through its Strategy and Data Strategy, and
to compliance with the government functional standards that apply to it, including GovS 010.

That commitment is what this playbook implements. GovS 010 asks for the levels of quality and
certainty required of analysis to be agreed and recorded, for the checks that deliver them to be
proportionate to the risk, and for someone to be accountable for each piece of analysis. Sections 5,
6 and 3 are those three things written down.
